vignette:
The Weight of That Night

Kofi is a 46-year-old Ghanaian-born curriculum designer who has lived in the United States for nearly fifteen years. He is soft-spoken and precise in the way he uses language - a quality that serves him well in his work, where he spends his days carefully sequencing learning objectives and crafting educational frameworks for a mid-sized nonprofit. He is married to a woman he describes as "the most patient person I have ever known," and together they have two teenage sons. On paper, his life looks ordered and purposeful. In the room with him, something else is visible - a man who has been quietly drowning for two years.

Two years ago, Kofi was driving home from a late work meeting when he was pulled over by two officers on a stretch of highway outside the city. He had done nothing wrong. What followed was forty-five minutes that he cannot fully explain to anyone, including himself. He was ordered out of the car, forced to the ground, his face pressed into the asphalt while one officer's knee held him down and the other searched his vehicle. He remembers the smell of the road, the cold of the pavement against his cheek, the sound of his own voice saying I am not resisting over and over as though repetition might protect him. He was eventually released without explanation, without apology, without charges. He drove home, walked into his kitchen, sat down at the table, and did not speak for the rest of the night.

He told his wife something had happened but could not say what for several days. He returned to work the following Monday and told no one. He opened his laptop and continued building a unit on civic engagement for middle schoolers, and he found the irony so unbearable that he had to close the document and sit in the bathroom for twenty minutes.

Since that night, Kofi has not been the same man, and he knows it. He sleeps in fragments. He wakes between two and four in the morning with his heart already pounding, his body certain that something is happening even when the bedroom is dark and still. His wife reaches for him and he flinches before he can stop himself. He hates that he flinches. He has begun sleeping on the couch some nights, telling her it is because he does not want to disturb her, which is partly true and partly a way of being alone with the thing that lives in him now.

He avoids driving after dark. He takes longer routes to avoid the highway where it happened. When he sees a police vehicle in his rearview mirror, even in daylight, his hands tighten on the wheel and his vision narrows and for a few seconds he is back on the ground, his cheek on the asphalt, saying words that no one was listening to. He has nearly rear-ended another car twice during these moments.

At work, he struggles to concentrate in ways that alarm him. He has always prided himself on precision - on the ability to hold a complex curriculum architecture in his mind and move through it methodically. Now he rereads the same paragraph four or five times. He misses deadlines he would never have missed before. His supervisor has asked twice, gently, if everything is all right. He says yes. He is a Black man who was pinned to the ground by police and released without explanation, and he says yes, everything is fine, because he does not yet have language for what it means to carry something this large inside a life that is supposed to look normal.

He describes a persistent feeling of being outside himself - watching his own days from a slight distance, present but not quite inhabiting the moments he moves through. He still attends his sons' soccer games. He still makes coffee in the morning. He still loves his wife. But he describes the man who does these things as someone he is watching, someone he is not entirely sure he can get back to.
